summary: Today’s pulse tracks Safety check calls after Irish teenager electrocuted taking shower in Greece, Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake kills at least 38 in Indonesia, and Eleven killed in Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon, authorities say. Across Guardian and BBC, the strongest repeated signals are addresses, arday, and calls. In the background, Tributes paid to Jason Arday after former Cambridge professor’s death and Met apologises for exposing 143 email addresses of Mohamed Al Fayed victims keep the wider picture in motion.

headlines.title: Safety check calls after Irish teenager electrocuted taking shower in Greece
headlines.description: Alex McKee died when picking up showerhead in ‘outdoor and rudimentary’ bathroom on Kimolos The death of an Irish teenager, electrocuted while taking a shower in a holiday home in Greece, has led to calls for tighter checks on appliances at tourist accommodation. Alex McKee, 17, is said to have died instantly when picking up the showerhead in a bathroom described as “outdoor and rudimentary” on Kimolos.

headlines.title: Powerful magnitude 7.7 earthquake kills at least 38 in Indonesia
headlines.description: A search and rescue operation is under way to find survivors in Flores, an island in eastern Indonesia.

headlines.title: Eleven killed in Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon, authorities say
headlines.description: Israel's military said it had struck "Hezbollah terror infrastructure" in response to what it described as an earlier action against its soldiers.

headlines.title: Tributes paid to Jason Arday after former Cambridge professor’s death
headlines.description: Andy Burnham calls for reflection after ‘a tragedy on so many levels’ in comments echoed by London mayor Sadiq Khan Andy Burnham has called the death of Jason Arday, who was found dead at his home in south London on Friday, a “tragedy on so many levels”. Arday resigned as a professor at the University of Cambridge last week after allegations of plagiarism, which he denied. He was pronounced dead just after 3pm on Friday .

headlines.title: Met apologises for exposing 143 email addresses of Mohamed Al Fayed victims
headlines.description: London police force tells Telegraph incident was result of ‘human error’ and it is conducting an investigation The Metropolitan police have apologised for accidentally exposing the email addresses of more than 140 victims of Mohamed Al Fayed. In a group update about its investigation into the former Harrods owner, the force copied the email addresses of 143 victims of Fayed in a message that included about 12 other recipients, the Telegraph reported.

headlines.title: ‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in England
headlines.description: In one court in Kent, most cases relate to term-time holidays, but non-attendance is a complex issue and post-pandemic rates remain high As the long school summer break approached its mid-point recently, Margate beach was crowded with families enjoying the brief reprieve between the year’s fourth and fifth heatwaves. For most, thoughts of the classroom were probably not at the forefront of their minds. But for the seven mothers and two fathers who were summoned at 10am to a stuffy room in the town’s magistrates court, set just behind the beachfront strip of arcades, the subject was unavoidable. They were among hundreds of parents due in courts across England this month for failing to ensure their children had regularly attended school over the course of the last academic year.

headlinePool.title: How to buy a ‘mega-dinghy’: the perilous new model of Channel crossing
headlinePool.description: Boats carrying hundreds of people are a clear and alarming trend. But where do such large vessels come from? Providing a large dinghy for use in the choppy seas of western Europe was not a problem, as long as the order was for more than 20 vessels, they said. The sales manager at the Chinese company even had an online brochure for an undercover Guardian reporter, posing as a prospective client, to peruse. They had a production capacity of 500 boats a month and, yes, it was possible to get even bigger ones for the right price. They could do a seven or even an eight-metre military-style dinghy for $1,678 (£1,238) a boat, without the engines, but that would be lacking CE certification, the mandatory mark that shows a product meets EU health and safety requirements. Additional reporting by Lyndon Li

headlinePool.title: So much solar: Digging into the list of every US power plant that went online this year
headlinePool.description: Utility-scale solar leads by a mile, followed by batteries. Fossil fuels, not so much.

headlinePool.title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial: prosecutors revive theory of faked suicide attempt
headlinePool.description: Prosecutors pointed to internet searches made on the family computer in the months before the killings to make their case Prosecutors revived a theory in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial case this week, suggesting she had faked a suicide attempt after allegedly strangling her three children. While prosecutors have been arguing that Clancy acted intentionally and should be held criminally responsible, her defense has said she suffered from postpartum psychosis.

headlinePool.title: US navy veterans and military health experts express concern over USS Abraham Lincoln sailors
headlinePool.description: Prolonged deployment is coupled with reports of water shortages, plumbing issues and attempts to jump overboard Trump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln US navy veterans and military health experts are expressing concerns about the strain on sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent nearly nine months at sea supporting US operations in the Middle East, amid reports of poor living conditions and worsening mental health among its crew. The San Diego-based aircraft carrier left port on 21 November, originally bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East as the US-Israel war with Iran began. It has now spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea without a significant port visit, with its deployment repeatedly extended.

headlinePool.title: UK’s biggest EV battery gigafactory shelves expansion as Jaguar Land Rover talks stall
headlinePool.description: Chinese-owned AESC has pushed back plans in sign of slowing transition from petrol and diesel to electric cars Andy Burnham moves to cut new EV sales targets The UK’s biggest gigafactory has shelved plans to expand production in Sunderland because of stalled talks on a deal to supply electric car batteries to Jaguar Land Rover. Chinese-owned AESC produces batteries for Nissan at its gigafactory next door to the Japanese carmaker’s Sunderland plant. However, AESC has had to push back its ramp-up plans because of lower-than-expected demand from Nissan and the lack of a deal with JLR, according to people with knowledge of the situation.

headlinePool.title: Double jeopardy could spell end of state case after Luigi Mangione’s guilty plea
headlinePool.description: Defense argues New York cannot try Mangione over same act or offense as federal case – the killing of Brian Thompson Luigi Mangione ’s plea to federal stalking charges in UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson’s death has spurred questions about the fate of the separate Manhattan murder case against him, with experts saying New York’s double-jeopardy law could derail that trial. Mangione pleaded guilty to one count of interstate stalking resulting in death, and one count of cyberstalking through use of interstate facilities resulting in death, in connection with the 4 December 2024 shooting outside a Midtown hotel. Both charges carry a potential maximum life sentence.

headlinePool.title: Family stranded at sea for 16 hours after jet ski capsized in Thailand
headlinePool.description: A father and his two young sons spent a night adrift before being rescued off the coast of the island of Koh Samui.

headlinePool.title: Israeli strikes on south Lebanon kill nine in worst toll since June
headlinePool.description: Two airstrikes reportedly hit homes in Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani with rescue services trying to find survivors Nine people have been killed, including three children, and 11 injured in two Israeli airstrikes on south Lebanon, the worst toll since deals in June brought a lull in hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Israeli warplanes bombed a home on the outskirts of the village of Ansar in southern Lebanon, killing seven people and flattening the building early on Saturday morning. Rescue services were working at the site to try to find survivors and locate bodies.

headlinePool.title: ICE detained a Venezuelan soccer pro. His case shows the immigration backlog crisis
headlinePool.description: Homero Calderón's detention by ICE spotlights the massive backlog in the U.S. immigration system.
